messages.content: I have a Google Pixel phone and I can't hear it ring from the other room. How do I make the ringer louder?

You can turn the ringer up with the buttons on the side of your phone.

1. Press one of the **volume buttons** on the side of your phone.
2. A small volume bar appears on the screen. Tap the **Menu** icon at the right.
3. Find **Ring Volume** and slide it up to make the ring louder.

If you don't see a **Menu** icon, your phone has older software. Tap the **Down arrow** at the right instead, then slide **Ring**.

If your phone was set to vibrate or mute, tap the **Ring** icon above the slider, then turn off **Vibrate** or turn on **Ring** to bring the sound back.

2. Tap the **Down arrow** at the right of the volume bar.
3. Find the **Ring** slider and slide it up to make calls ring louder.

If you would rather use the Settings app, you can also open **Settings** and tap **Sound**.

messages.content: My iPhone has no home button, you just look at it to unlock it. How do I take a screenshot of my boarding pass?

On your iPhone you take a screenshot with two buttons on the sides.

1. Open the screen you want to capture, such as your boarding pass.
2. Press the **side button** and the **volume up button** at the same time.
3. Let go of both buttons quickly.

On iOS 18 or earlier, a small picture of your screenshot appears in the lower-left corner for a moment. On iOS 26, the screenshot appears right away with tools you can use.

You can find it later in **Photos**. Tap **Collections**, then **Media Types**, then **Screenshots**.

messages.content: My nephew put a bunch of add-ons into my web browser last summer, some coupon thing and a shopping helper and I don't know what else. Ever since then, when I go to Gmail on my desktop computer, the page just sits there and never opens. My internet is fine because I can read the news. I don't want to call him again. What could be causing it and how do I fix it?

Those add-ons (called extensions) could be the cause. You can check them one at a time.

1. Turn off one extension in your browser.
2. Open Gmail again and see if it loads.
3. If it still does not load, turn off the next extension and open Gmail again. Repeat until Gmail loads.

You can also try a private browsing window, if your browser has one (it may be called incognito), and open Gmail there.

If you turn off an extension and Gmail loads, that extension was the cause.

messages.content: Gmail will not open on my laptop in my web browser. The last time I deleted a program, the whole computer went wrong, so please do not tell me to uninstall anything or take any programs off. I only want to try the gentle things. Which ones are those?

Here are gentle things to try. None of them remove any programs.

1. Update your browser to the latest version, then open Gmail again.
2. Try a different browser and open Gmail there.
3. Restart your laptop and open Gmail again.
4. Turn your Wi-Fi off, then back on, and open Gmail again.

If your browser has a private window (it may be called incognito), you can open Gmail there too.

3. Open Gmail again.

If it still will not load, tell me and we'll try the next step.

1. Restart your router. The router's manual has instructions on how.
2. Open Gmail again.
3. If it still will not load, connect to a different network, if you have one nearby, and open Gmail there.

If the connection keeps having trouble, contact your internet service provider, or whoever runs your Wi-Fi network.

messages.content: My printer is plugged into my Windows computer with a USB cable but nothing comes out when I press print. What should I check?

Let's start with two simple things.

1. Turn off the printer and unplug it from the wall.
2. Wait 30 seconds.
3. Plug the printer back in and turn it on.
4. Check the USB cable. Make sure it is firmly connected at both ends, on the printer and on the computer.
5. Try printing again.

If your printer shows an error, check for low ink or paper, an open cover, or a paper jam.

If it still does not print, tell me and we'll try the next step.

messages.content: I'm staying at my daughter's house this weekend. She wrote the Wi-Fi name and password on a card for me. The network is called SmithHome. I have an iPhone 13 with the latest update. How do I get my phone on her internet?

Here's how to connect your iPhone to SmithHome. Keep the card with the password nearby. This takes about two minutes.

1. Open the **Settings** app.
2. Tap **Wi-Fi**.
3. Make sure Wi-Fi is turned on.
4. Tap **SmithHome** in the list.
5. Type the password from the card if it asks.
6. Confirm the connection.

When you're connected, you'll see a blue tick next to **SmithHome**, and the Wi-Fi icon at the top corner of the screen.

If you don't see SmithHome in the list, move closer to the internet box in her home and check again.
I don't see SmithHome in the list at all.

Let's check a few things. Try them in order, and stop as soon as **SmithHome** appears in the list.

1. **Check the exact name.** Ask your daughter to check the network name. It might be slightly different, like **SmithHome-5G**.
2. **Ask whether other phones work.** Ask your daughter whether other phones in the house can connect.
3. **Check the internet box.** Make sure the router is plugged in and its lights are on.
4. **Move closer** to the router, then look at the list again.
5. **Check Airplane Mode.** In **Settings**, make sure **Airplane Mode** is turned off.
6. **Check the Wi-Fi switch.** If it looks gray and you can't tap it, restart your iPhone.
7. **Restart the router.** Unplug the router and the modem, then plug them back in. Ask your daughter first, because this turns off the internet for everyone in the house for a few minutes.

If SmithHome still doesn't show up, tell me which network names you do see.

messages.content: I got a Facebook message from someone who says she is my granddaughter Emily. She wrote that she is stuck in another country, lost her bag, and needs me to wire her money today or she can't get home. The picture looks like her but the writing sounds a bit odd. I want to help her but I'm not sure. What should I do?

I'm glad you stopped to ask. **Please don't wire any money yet.** Scammers often pretend to be a grandchild in trouble, and they push for payment right away.

1. Take a breath. You don't have to act right now, even if the story sounds dramatic.
2. Call Emily on a phone number **you know is really hers**. Don't use any number from the message.
3. Check the story with another trusted family member too.
4. Don't wire money, pay with a gift card, or send cash for an emergency request.

You can report the message at **www.ftc.gov/complaint**.

sources.title: FTC: Talking Turkey (family emergency scams)

messages.content: A man called saying he is my grandson Kevin and he was in a car accident. He said a lawyer will call me for the bail money, and he begged me not to tell his parents because they'd be so angry. His mother is traveling and I can't reach her right now. He says there's no time. Should I do what he asks?

**Please don't send any money yet.** A caller who begs for secrecy and says there is no time is a common sign of a family emergency scam. A fake lawyer is another sign.

1. Hang up and take your time. There is no need to rush.
2. Call Kevin on a number **you know is genuine**.
3. If you can't reach his mother, check the story with **another trusted family member**, even though the caller asked you to keep it secret.
4. Don't wire money, pay with a gift card, or send cash.

sources.title: FTC: Talking Turkey (family emergency scams)

messages.content: My mother is 84 and just told me someone called saying he was her grandson and needed money fast for bail. She hasn't sent anything but she is shaken. How can I help her?

It's good she told you before sending anything. Here is how to help her.

1. Reassure her. These calls are built to make people panic, and the caller pushes for money right away.
2. Help her call her grandson on a number you know is genuine.
3. Check the story with another trusted family member, even if the caller asked for secrecy.
4. Remind her not to wire money, pay with a gift card, or send cash for an emergency request.
5. Report the call at **www.ftc.gov/complaint**.

It also helps to agree as a family that no one will ever call with an emergency request for wired money, gift card payment, or cash.

sources.title: FTC: Talking Turkey (family emergency scams)

messages.content: My friend was just fooled by a call from a fake grandchild. How can I tell if a call like that is a scam in the future?

Here are the signs of this kind of scam:

1. The caller says they are a family member in an emergency, such as needing bail or medical care.
2. They say things like "I know I don't sound like myself" or "Don't tell Mom. Let's keep this our secret."
3. A doctor, lawyer, or police officer may be part of the story.
4. They want money **right away**, by wire, gift card, or cash.

What to do if it happens:
1. Don't act right away, however dramatic the story is.
2. Call your relative on a number you know is genuine.
3. Check with another trusted family member.

Agree with your family that no one will ever call with an emergency request for wired money, gift cards, or cash. You can report scams at **www.ftc.gov/complaint**.

messages.content: Oh no. I think I got scammed. A woman said my grandson was in jail and I mailed $1,500 cash to an address she gave me. Now I called my grandson's real number and he is fine. What do I do now?

I'm sorry this happened. It is not your fault, and you did the right thing by calling your grandson.

1. **Don't send any more money**, even if the caller contacts you again.
2. Tell another trusted family member what happened so you have support.
3. Report it to the FTC at **www.ftc.gov/complaint**.

messages.content: A woman phoned me saying she works in the fraud department at my bank and that someone is trying to take money out of my account. She was very polite and said she would text me a code to stop it, and I just need to read the code back to her. I'm worried about my savings. Is this real?

**Please don't read her the code.** This is a known scam. Scammers pretend to be someone you trust and claim there is a problem with your account. With the code, they can log in and move your money.

1. Hang up. Don't argue with her.
2. Block the number.
3. If you're worried about your account, contact your bank directly. Use a number you trust, like the one on your statement or in your app. Don't use any number the caller gave you.
4. Report the call at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

Remember that anyone who asks for your verification code is a scammer.

messages.content: A man keeps calling and texting me. He already knows my full name and the town I live in, and he sounds very kind. **Please don't tell him the code.** Scammers often know details about you and sound sympathetic. That is part of how they earn your trust. Anyone who asks you for your verification code is a scammer.

1. Don't engage. Hang up and stop texting him.
2. Block his number.
3. If you're worried about your accounts, contact your bank, credit union, or investment advisor directly. Use a number you trust, such as the one on your statement or in your app.
4. Report him at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

Never call back a number he gave you.

1. **Never give a verification code to anyone.** Anyone who asks for it is a scammer.
2. If someone asks, don't engage. Hang up, block the number, and stop texting.
3. If he is worried about an account, he should contact his bank, credit union, or investment advisor directly, using a number he trusts, like the one on his statement or in his app.

messages.content: How do these verification code scams work, and how can I stay safe from them?

Here is how they work. Scammers pretend to be someone you trust and say there is a problem with an account or that your identity was stolen. They may know details about you and sound sympathetic. Then they ask for your verification code. With it, they can log in to your account and move money out of savings or investment accounts.

How to stay safe:

1. **Never give your verification code to anyone.**
2. Remember that anyone who asks for it is a scammer.
3. If someone asks, hang up, block the number, and stop texting.
4. If you're worried, contact your bank directly using a number on your statement or in your app.
5. Report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

2. Don't call back any number the man gave you. It would take you to the scammer.

messages.content: I found a beautiful rocking chair on a website I've never heard of, and the price is half what stores charge. They only accept cryptocurrency and say it's because of fees. My nephew says no but I really want it. Is it safe to pay them that way?

1. Don't send money to anyone who says you can only pay one specific way.
2. Search online for the website's name with words like "review," "scam," or "complaint."
3. If the seller accepts a **credit card**, that is safer. Credit cards have more protections and let you dispute charges.

messages.content: is it safe to pay for something online?

It can be, but it depends on what you're buying, who you're buying from, and how they want you to be paid.

**What are you trying to buy, and how is the seller asking you to pay** (for example a credit card, a gift card, or a bank transfer)?

One quick tip while you check: if a seller says you can only pay with **gift cards, a wire transfer, or cryptocurrency**, stop. That's a common sign of a scam.
I'm buying a used lawn mower from a man on a website and he says I have to pay with a gift card.

**Please don't pay with a gift card.** When someone says gift card is the only way to pay, that is a sign of a scam. The same goes for a bank transfer, wire transfer, cryptocurrency, or a payment app.

1. Don't send money to anyone who says you can only pay one specific way, whatever reason they give.
2. Search online for the seller's name with words like "review," "scam," or "complaint" and see what others say.
3. If you decide to buy, pay by **credit card** whenever possible. It has more protections and lets you dispute charges.

You can report a seller like this at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Alert: A way to spot scams: how someone asks you to pay

messages.content: What are the warning signs that someone is trying to scam me when I buy things online?

The biggest warning sign is how they ask you to pay.

1. If someone says the **only** way to pay is a bank transfer, wire transfer, cryptocurrency, payment app, or gift card, it is probably a scam.
2. Never send money to anyone who says you can only pay one specific way, whatever reason they give.
3. Check the seller. Search online for the name with words like "review," "scam," or "complaint."
4. Pay by **credit card** whenever possible. It has more protections and lets you dispute charges.

If you already paid a scammer, contact the company you used to send the money right away, tell them it was fraud, and ask if they can stop or reverse it. You can report scams at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

messages.content: How do I make the text bigger on my iPhone? Everything is too small to read.

You can make the text bigger in Settings. It takes about a minute, and you can change it back anytime.

1. Open the **Settings** app. Its icon is a gray gear.
2. Tap **Display & Brightness**.
3. Tap **Text Size**.
4. Drag the slider at the bottom of the screen to the right.

The sample text changes as you drag, so you can stop when it's easy to read.

If you need it even bigger, go to **Settings**, then **Accessibility**, then **Display & Text Size**, then **Larger Text**, and drag that slider. Very large text can make some buttons harder to tap, so slide it back a little if that happens.
I made it really big and now some of the buttons are cut off and hard to tap.

That can happen when the text is set very large. Let's make it a little smaller so the buttons fit again.

1. Open **Settings**.
2. Tap **Display & Brightness**.
3. Tap **Text Size**.
4. Drag the slider **one step to the left**.
5. Go back to the app and check the buttons.

If you made the text bigger with **Larger Text** instead, the slider is in **Settings**, then **Accessibility**, then **Display & Text Size**, then **Larger Text**.

Repeat until the buttons fit on the screen and the text is still easy for you to read.

messages.content: My grandson called from a number I don't know, sounding scared, and said he'd been in a car accident and needs $2,000 sent through Western Union. He begged me not to tell his parents. I've tried his own phone but it goes straight to voicemail.

2. **Call him again** at the number you already know is his, not the number that called you.
3. Since you can't reach him, **contact him through another family member or his friends**. That includes his parents, even though the caller asked you not to tell them.

Asking you to wire money, send cryptocurrency, or buy gift cards are warning signs, because those payments are hard to get back.

You can report the call at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

messages.content: I got a text about a package, is it real?
Let's check it together. For now, **please don't click any link or give any information** in that text. **What does the text ask you to do?**
It has a link and says I need to pay $1.99 for redelivery.

Thanks. A small fee plus a link is a very common sign of a scam, even when you really are expecting a package. Please **don't click the link**. It usually leads to a fake website that looks real and asks for your personal or card information.

Instead:

1. **Don't click** the link or reply.
2. Check on your package using the website or app of the **store where you bought it**. Go there directly, not through the text.
3. **Report the text.** Use your phone's **junk** or **spam** reporting option if you see one, or forward the text to **7726**. You can also report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.
4. Then delete it.

If you already clicked and typed in your card number, call your bank right away using the number on the back of your card.

messages.content: I got an email from my pastor asking me to buy five $100 gift cards for church members and send him the numbers on the back. He said he's in a meeting and can't talk. Should I do it?

Please **don't buy the gift cards**. This is a common scam. Real businesses, government agencies, and people you know don't ask to be paid with gift card numbers, and once you share the numbers, the money is very hard to get back.

Here's what to do:

1. **Don't reply** to the email.
2. **Call your pastor** using a phone number you already have, or call the church office, and ask if he really sent it.
3. If it's fake, you can report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

**If you already bought cards and shared the numbers:**
- Call the **gift card company** right away and ask for your money back. Sometimes they can freeze what's left on the card.
- Keep the cards and the store receipt.
- Report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

I'm sorry this happened. This scam fools a lot of careful people. Acting quickly gives you the best chance of getting money back.

1. **Contact the gift card company right away.** Tell them the cards were used in a scam and ask for your money back. Sometimes they can freeze money that hasn't been spent yet. The FTC's gift card scam page lists contact information for major gift card companies.
2. **Keep the cards and the store receipt**, and take a photo of both. You'll need them when you report it.
3. **Report the scam** at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.
4. **Don't reply** to the email, and don't buy more cards, even if you're asked again.
5. **Tell your church office**, so they can warn other members, and let your pastor know his email may have been hacked.

messages.content: I lost my iPhone at the park. I don't own any other Apple things, no iPad, no Mac. I only have an old Windows laptop at home. Can I still look for my phone?

Yes, you can use the laptop's web browser.

1. Go to **icloud.com/find**.
2. Sign in with your Apple Account.
3. Open the device list under **All Devices** and choose your iPhone.
4. From there, you can **play a sound**, **mark it as lost**, or erase it.

4. Add your contact info and a message.

messages.content: I met a man online three months ago. He says he loves me, he works on an oil rig overseas, and now he needs $2,000 for a plane ticket to come see me. Should I send it?

I'm glad you asked before sending anything. Please **don't send the money**. What you're describing matches a very common scam called a **romance scam**.

**Warning signs:**
- The person can't meet in person, often saying they work far away, like on an **oil rig** or in the military.
- Strong feelings grow quickly through lots of messages.
- Now there's a **need for money**, like travel costs or an emergency.

**What to do:**
1. **Don't send money or gift cards** to someone you haven't met in person.
2. **Talk to a friend or family member** you trust. People close to you can often spot things that are hard to see from the inside.
3. You can **search his photo** online to see if it appears under other names. I can show you how.
4. If it's a scam, stop contact and report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov** and to the website or app where you met.

If you've already sent money, contact your bank or the payment company right away and ask for a refund.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: What To Know About Romance Scams

messages.content: I already sent $500 in gift cards to a man I met online. I read the PINs to him over the phone. Now he wants more. What do I do?

1. Contact the gift card company right away. Tell them you paid a scammer and ask for a refund.
2. Report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.
3. Tell the site or app where you met him.
4. Talk to a trusted friend or family member about what happened.

Gift cards are one of the hard-to-reverse ways scammers ask for money, so acting quickly matters.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: What You Need to Know About Romance Scams

messages.content: A caller said he's from Social Security and my number has been suspended because of a crime. He wants me to buy gift cards to fix it. What should I do?

Please **hang up and don't pay anything**. This is a scam. The real Social Security Administration **won't threaten you, won't suspend your Social Security number, and won't ask you to pay with gift cards**.

**What to do:**
1. **Hang up.** Don't share any personal or bank information.
2. Don't trust caller ID. Scammers can make it show a government name or number.
3. If you're worried, **call Social Security yourself** using the phone number on its official website, not a number the caller gave you.
4. **Report the call** to the Social Security Administration's Office of the Inspector General and to the FTC at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

If you already shared your Social Security number or bank details, go to **IdentityTheft.gov** for next steps, and tell me so I can help.

messages.content: I'm making a new password for my insurance company's website and it keeps rejecting my long phrase of words because it has a length limit. I also don't trust password manager programs and don't want one. How can I still make a strong password?

You can still make a strong one without a password manager. When a site rejects long passwords, **mix different kinds of characters** instead.

1. Use **uppercase and lowercase letters**, **numbers**, and **symbols** together.
2. Make it as long as the site allows. Aim for at least 12 characters if you can.
3. Don't use a common phrase, song lyric, or movie quote.

Your **email** password matters most, because password reset links often go to your email inbox.

messages.content: An online store emailed me that it lost its customers' passwords in a data breach. I use the same password for that store and for my email and my bank. What should I do?

1. At the store, **create a new strong password**. Make it long, at least 12 characters. Several random words work well.
2. Change the password on your **email** and your **bank** account too, since they share the old one.
3. If you see that someone is using your personal information, get help at **IdentityTheft.gov**.

Email is the most important one to protect, because password reset links often go there.

messages.content: What is Stolen Device Protection on iPhone and how do I turn it on?

Stolen Device Protection adds extra security if someone steals your iPhone **and** knows your passcode. When your phone is away from familiar places like home or work, it requires **Face ID or Touch ID** for things like using saved passwords, and it adds a **one-hour wait** before important changes, like changing your Apple Account password.

**To turn it on:**
1. Open **Settings**.
2. Tap **Face ID & Passcode** (or **Touch ID & Passcode**).
3. Enter your passcode.
4. Tap **Stolen Device Protection** and turn it on.

It may already be on, so check first.

It needs a few things to work: an iPhone updated to **iOS 17.3 or later**, a passcode, Face ID or Touch ID, two-factor authentication on your Apple Account, **Find My** turned on, and **Significant Locations** turned on in Location Services.

When your phone is away from familiar places like home or work, it requires **Face ID or Touch ID** for things like using saved passwords, and it adds a **one-hour wait** before important changes, like changing your Apple Account password.

**To turn it on:**
1. Open **Settings**.
2. Tap **Face ID & Passcode** (or **Touch ID & Passcode**).
3. Enter your passcode.
4. Tap **Stolen Device Protection** and turn it on.

It may already be on, so check first.

It needs a few things to work: an iPhone updated to **iOS 17.3 or later**, a passcode, Face ID or Touch ID, two-factor authentication on your Apple Account, **Find My** turned on, and **Significant Locations** turned on in Location Services.

messages.content: Why does my iPhone stop charging at 80% overnight? Is something wrong with it?

Most likely nothing is wrong. This is usually a feature called **Optimized Battery Charging**. It holds the battery at 80% during long charges, like overnight, to slow down battery wear. Your iPhone then finishes charging around the time you usually unplug it.

A couple of other things can also stop charging at 80%:
- **Heat:** if your iPhone gets too warm, it may pause charging above 80%. Moving it to a cooler spot helps.
- **Charge limit:** on iPhone 15 and newer, a charge limit setting may be turned on. You can change it if you want a full charge.

If you need a full charge right away, tell me and I'll walk you through it.

messages.content: My iPhone only vibrates when someone calls. It doesn't ring. How do I fix that?

messages.content: I get too many newsletter emails in Gmail. How do I unsubscribe on my computer?

Gmail can unsubscribe you in a couple of clicks. It takes a few seconds per sender.

1. Go to **mail.google.com**.
2. Open an email from the sender.
3. Click **Unsubscribe** next to the sender's name at the top.
4. Click **Unsubscribe** again in the box that pops up.

If you see **Go to website** instead, that sender needs you to unsubscribe on their own site.

To see all your subscriptions at once, click **More** on the left side, then **Manage subscriptions**.

If you're not sure an email is from a sender you trust, don't reply or open any links in it. It can take a few days for the emails to stop.

messages.content: I accidentally deleted an important email in Gmail. How do I get it back? I'm on my computer.

2. On the left side, click **More**, then click **Trash**.
3. Find the email and check the box next to it.
4. At the top, click **Move to**.

Emails stay in Trash for up to 30 days. After that, they're deleted for good and can't be recovered.

messages.content: My iPhone is frozen and won't respond when I touch it. What do I do?

You can **force restart** it. The steps depend on your model.

**iPhone with Face ID (no Home button):**
1. Press and quickly release the **volume up** button.
2. Press and quickly release the **volume down** button.
3. Press and **hold** the **side button** until you see the **Apple logo**. This can take more than 10 seconds, so keep holding.

**iPhone 7:** press and hold the **side button** and **volume down** together until you see the Apple logo.

**iPhone 6s or older (with a Home button):** press and hold the **Home button** and the **side or top button** together for about 10 seconds, until you see the Apple logo.

If it still won't turn on, charge it for an hour and try again.

messages.content: My iPhone won't charge when I plug it in. What should I try?

Let's go through a few checks. This can take up to an hour, mostly waiting.

1. **Restart your iPhone.**
2. **Check the cable and adapter** for damage, like breakage or bent prongs. Don't use a damaged one.
3. **Plug into a wall outlet** and make sure the cable, adapter, and outlet are firmly connected, or try a different outlet.
4. **Look in the charging port** on the bottom of the phone. If there's lint or dirt, carefully clear it out, then plug in firmly again.
5. **Leave it charging for half an hour.**
6. If it still won't turn on or only shows a battery picture, **force restart** it. On an iPhone 8 or later:
   - Press and quickly release **volume up**.
   - Press and quickly release **volume down**.
   - Press and hold the **side button** until you see the **Apple logo**.
   On an older iPhone, tell me the model and I'll give you those steps.
7. **Charge it for another half hour.**

If none of this works, it may need service from Apple.

**If it stops at 80%:** that's usually a battery-saving feature, not a problem.

messages.content: A man I met online says he is an investment manager and wants me to buy cryptocurrency and send it to his site. He says I will make a lot of money. Is this real?

Please do not buy or send any cryptocurrency. This is very likely a scam.

Scammers promise easy profits and steer people to send crypto to a fake investment account. The site can look real, but you may never be able to take your money out.

1. Do not click any more links from him or pay him.
2. Search his name and the crypto name with words like **review**, **scam**, or **complaint**.
3. Report him at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

Nobody can truly guarantee profits.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: What To Know About Cryptocurrency and Scams

messages.content: I got a text yesterday saying it was from the power company. It said my account has a legal problem and I have to buy cryptocurrency and send it today or they will shut off my power. I am a widow and I live alone and I am scared. I have not done anything yet. What should I do?

Do not pay, and do not click the link in that text. Only scammers demand payment in cryptocurrency.

Scammers pretend to be utilities or government offices, claim there is a problem, and tell you to buy crypto to fix it. You have done nothing wrong.

1. Do not click any links in the text, even if it looks like it is from a company you know.
2. Do not send any money to the person who contacted you.
3. Report the text at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.

sources.title: FTC Consumer Advice: What To Know About Cryptocurrency and Scams

messages.content: A woman on a dating app has been teaching me to invest in crypto. Her website shows my money has doubled. She says I must add more by tonight or I lose my profits, but when I tried to take some out it would not let me. What do I do?

Do not add any more money. This looks like an investment scam.

The site can look real but be fake, and scammers often make it hard to withdraw. A love interest who gives investment advice is a warning sign, and so is pressure to pay someone who contacted you first.

1. Stop sending money and stop clicking her links.
2. Report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.
3. You can also report it at **sec.gov/tcr** and **CFTC.gov/complaint**.
4. If you sent crypto already, contact the exchange you used.

messages.content: How can I tell if a crypto investment offer is a scam, and where do I report one?

Never pay anyone who contacts you out of the blue and asks for crypto. Only scammers demand payment in cryptocurrency.

1. Guaranteed profits or big, quick returns.
2. Unexpected contact from a company, agency, or "investment manager".
3. A love interest who gives investment advice or asks for money.
4. Vague explanations of how the investment works.

Do not click links in unexpected texts, emails, or social media messages. Before investing, search the name and the crypto name with words like **review**, **scam**, or **complaint**.

messages.content: I already sent a lot of cryptocurrency to a person I met on social media for an investment. Now they want more money to let me withdraw. Can I get my money back?

2. Report it at **ReportFraud.ftc.gov**.
3. Also report it at **CFTC.gov/complaint**, **sec.gov/tcr**, and **ic3.gov/Home/FileComplaint**.

messages.content: How do I set up Time Machine to back up my Mac? I just bought an external hard drive.

messages.content: My Google Pixel phone won't charge. I plug it in and nothing seems to happen.

Let's check the usual causes.

1. Take the phone case off so it does not block the plug.
2. Make sure the cable is pushed in firmly at both ends, the adapter and the phone.
3. Look in the phone's charging port for dust or lint.
4. Try a different cable or adapter, and a different wall outlet.
5. Leave it plugged in for one minute. A battery icon on the screen means the phone is off and charging.
6. Press and hold the **Power** button for 5 to 7 seconds.

A very low battery can take several minutes before the screen turns on.

messages.content: My Android phone says it has no internet. Web pages won't load. What should I do?

Try these in order.

1. Restart your phone.
2. Open **Settings** and tap **Network & internet** (on some phones it is called **Connections**).
3. Turn Wi-Fi off and mobile data on, and see if things load. If not, turn mobile data off and Wi-Fi on, and check again.
4. Turn **Airplane mode** on, wait 10 seconds, then turn it off.
5. If you use home Wi-Fi, unplug the router, wait 30 seconds, plug it back in, and wait about 30 seconds for the lights to come back.

If problems continue, contact your mobile service provider or your internet provider.

My daughter's tablet in the next room is fine though, or at least it was an hour ago. I've had the same Wi-Fi for years. I restarted the phone once already. What else can I try?

Here is what to try next for Wi-Fi.

1. Open **Settings** and tap **Network & Internet** (or **Connections**), then tap **Wi-Fi**.
2. Make sure **Wi-Fi** is turned on.
3. Look at the Wi-Fi symbol at the top of the screen. If it is missing or has no bars filled, you may be out of range. Move closer to the router and try again.
4. Restart the router. Unplug it and make sure the lights go out. Wait 30 seconds, plug it back in, and wait about 30 seconds for all the lights to come back.

If it still does not work, contact your internet provider.

messages.content: None of my texts are going through in Google Messages on my Android phone. What should I check?

messages.content: I heard my Android phone can lock itself if someone grabs it out of my hand and runs. How do I turn that on?

That is the **Theft Detection Lock** setting. Here is how to turn it on:

1. Open the **Settings** app.
2. Tap **Google**.
3. Tap **All services**.
4. Under **Personal & device safety**, tap **Theft protection**.

Set a screen lock first, because the setting won't turn on without one. If it is grayed out, your phone doesn't support it.

messages.content: I have a Samsung Galaxy and I don't own a computer, so I can't plug it into anything. Before I update, I would also like to know what the update changes. Can I see that on the phone?

Yes, you can see that on the phone, and you do not need a computer.

To see what the update includes:
1. Swipe down with two fingers from the top right corner, then tap the **Settings** icon.
2. Swipe to **Software update** (or **System updates**) and tap it.
3. Tap **Last update**, then tap **All changes**.

To update on the phone:
1. Go back to **Software update** (or **System updates**).
2. Tap **Download and install**. On some phones you may need to tap **Download now**.
3. When it finishes downloading, follow the instructions on the screen.

Note that you cannot use the phone while it installs, and that includes emergency calls.

messages.content: My Windows 11 laptop says the drive is almost full. How can I clear some space?

Windows has a cleanup tool that shows what you can safely remove. Here is how to use it:

1. Select **Start**, then **Settings**.
2. Select **System**, then **Storage**.
3. Select **Cleanup recommendations**.
4. Look at the groups: **Temporary files**, **Large or unused files**, **Files synced to the cloud**, and **Unused apps**. Tick the items you want to remove. Windows shows how much space each one will save.
5. Select the **Clean up** button in each section.

If you want to see how much room you have, open **File Explorer**, select **This PC**, and look under **Devices and drives**.

1. Open Google Maps in your browser, then click **Directions**.
2. Enter a starting point and a destination. You can type an address, type a place name, or click on the map.
3. Choose **Driving**.

The best route shows in blue, and other routes show in gray. Under the route, click **Details** to see the steps.

messages.content: I'd like bus directions to the farmers market on Google Maps on my computer.

Here is how to get bus directions:

1. Open Google Maps in your browser, then click **Directions**.
2. Enter your starting point and the farmers market as the destination.
3. Choose **Transit**.
I don't see any bus or transit option for my town.

Transit only shows where your city's transit agency has added its route information to Google Maps. Your agency may not have added it yet. You can still choose **Driving** or **Walking** from the same screen to get directions.

messages.content: I'm in a Zoom meeting on my laptop and I'd like to see captions of what people are saying. How do I turn them on?

Here is how to show captions in the Zoom app on your computer.

1. In the bar of buttons at the bottom of the meeting, click the **Show captions** icon.
2. If you do not see it, click **More** in that bar, then click **Show captions**.

The words people say will appear above the meeting buttons, with each speaker's name in front.

If you cannot turn captions on, the host may have restricted them. Click **More**, then **Request captions**, then click **Send**. The host or a co-host has to approve your request before captions appear.

messages.content: My granddaughter set up Zoom on my Android phone so I can join my church group. I'm hard of hearing and some people talk quietly, so I'm hoping to read what they say on the screen. I'm already in the meeting right now. Where do I find the captions?

You can show captions in the Zoom app on your phone like this.

1. Tap **More** in the buttons along the bottom of the meeting screen.
2. Tap **Show CC**.

The words people say will appear above the meeting buttons.

If you do not see **Show CC**, the host may have limited captions. Tap **More**, then **Request captions**, then **Send**. The host or a co-host has to approve your request.

messages.content: I'm on Zoom on my Windows computer. I want captions, but the letters are tiny and my eyes are bad. I only want to make the letters bigger for me, not change anything for the other people in the meeting. Can that be done?

Yes. These changes only affect your own screen.

1. Click the **Show captions** icon in the buttons at the bottom of the meeting. If you do not see it, click **More**, then **Show captions**.
2. Move your mouse over the captions and click the gear icon.
3. Click **Caption settings**. A panel called **Accessibility** opens on the right.
4. Drag the **Font size** slider to make the letters bigger.

If nothing happens when you click **Show captions**, the host may have restricted them. Click **More**, then **Request captions**, then **Send**. The host or a co-host has to approve your request.

sources.title: Zoom Support: Viewing captions in a meeting or webinar
